catalog_quote: 3.5 Word-stress. Word-stress is almost always laid on the penultimate syllable. This stress is strikingly strong, much more so than in modern Indonesian. Of course the stress shifts backwards, if a word is suffixed. For people not accustomed to such stress-shift the understandability of a spoken text suffers considerably by it. Generally the penult with a pepet is also stressed. The only exceptions I know are tambedol and tamberoq (kinds of fishes), which have the primary stress on the last syllable. However, during my short visit to Tanjoh, Lombok, I had the impression that in several cases words with a pepet before a geminate consonant were stressed on the last syllable. With regard to my remarks under 3.4.2.1 I was rather taken aback. Further checking is also necessary here. ... [3.4.2.3] Also in suffixed forms, in which consequently the stress shifts backwards, the doubled consonant…

new_statements.quote: Di dalam bahasa Bajau ditemukan adanya tekanan (stress), nada (pitch), dan perpanjangan (length), tetapi semuanya tidak fonemis. Di atas telah dijelaskan bahwa fonem-fonem hambat /p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/ dan /g/ serta fonem-fonem /m/, /n/, /s/, dan /l/ akan digandakan apabila didahului oleh suku yang bertekanan. Penggandaan fonem-fonem tersebut berarti suatu perpanjangan pada fonem yang bersangkutan, tetapi penggandaan atau perpanjangan fonem tersebut ternyata tidak akan mengubah arti. [pp. 24-25] ... 3) Fonem-fonem /p, t, k, b, d, g/, /m, n, s/, dan /l/ diucapkan ganda apabila didahului oleh suku yang bertekanan, seperti pada contoh berikut: /sapi/ 'sapi' [sappi]; /etuh/ 'itu' [ettuh]; /teke/ 'datang' [tekke]; /jela/ 'jala' [jella] [p. 23]
new_statements.translation: In Bajau, stress, pitch and length are found, but none of them is phonemic. It was explained above that the stop phonemes /p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/ and /g/ and the phonemes /m/, /n/, /s/ and /l/ are doubled when preceded by a stressed syllable. The doubling of these phonemes means a lengthening of the phoneme concerned, but this doubling or lengthening turns out not to change the meaning. ... 3) The phonemes /p, t, k, b, d, g/, /m, n, s/ and /l/ are pronounced double when preceded by a stressed syllable, as in the following examples: /sapi/ 'cow' [sappi]; /etuh/ 'that' [ettuh]; /teke/ 'come' [tekke]; /jela/ 'net' [jella].

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Not in the 'works' list (the task said not to add works); checked because a quote was claimed. File : sec. 3.2 Fonem Suprasegmental is on printed pp. 25-26 (pdf pp. 40-41), not 24-25; the quoted sentences are there verbatim apart from scanned noise. Rule 3) is on printed p. 23 (pdf p. 38) as stated, but the printed phonetic forms carry acute stress marks that the reader's transcription drops: [sáppi], [éttuh], [tékke], [jélla] (penult marked). What the reader missed is rule 4) on the same page as the quote, printed p. 24 (pdf p. 39): 'Vokal pada suku tertutup yang mendapat tekanan akan diucapkan sebagai diftong apabila konsonan penutupnya /k/ atau /ng/' with examples /kuning/ [kunieng], /la…
new_statements.relation_note: Bajau of Rampa, Kotabaru, South Kalimantan (a different variety from the NTB, Flores Sea and Kangean Bajo of the four listed works). Compatible with the catalog's penultimate rule (all cited stressed syllables are penults) and adds that stress is non-contrastive and conditions consonant gemination. Included because it was already downloaded into this item's check folder and is the only source held by the project with an explicit stress statement; it was not in the 'works' list.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is stated to exist but to be non-phonemic (as are pitch and length). Its position is not stated in words, but every example of a 'stressed syllable' that triggers gemination of the following consonant is the penult of a disyllable (sa- in sapi, e- in etuh, te- in teke, je- in jela), so the placement the description implies is penultimate; no secondary stress or exceptions are mentioned.
new_statements.identity_note: Each source describes a different Sama/Bajau community under indo1317: Husnan et al. 2015 = Bajo Pulo, Kec. Sape, Kab. Bima (Sumbawa, NTB); Candrawati et al. 1997 = Tanjung Luar, Kec. Keruak, Kab. Lombok Timur (NTB), said to derive from Sulawesi; Nuraini 2010 = 'Indonesian Bajo' of the Flores Sea (Kangean, SE Sulawesi, Sumbawa, Flores); Nuraini-Grangé 2008 = Kangean archipelago (Sumenep, East Java); the extra Hapip et al. 1979 = Bajau of Rampa, Kotabaru, South Kalimantan. Also a citation correction: Nuraini 2010 'Lexicon and word formation in Indonesian Bajo' is a Wacana 12(2) article (doi 10.17510/wjhi.v12i2.120), not a chapter in Benjamins LA 167.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Within the listed works: nothing. All three opened files were searched for tekan/ekanan/aksen/tonasi/supraseg/prosodi/stress/accent/prominence/prosody/tone/penult and read at the phonology chapters; they are silent on word stress as reported, and the 2008 thesis is confirmed inaccessible (theses.fr accessible=non, no HAL deposit). In the extra source the reader added (Hapip, Darmansyah & Noor 1979, Bahasa Bajau, South Kalimantan; not in the works list): rule 4 on printed p. 24 (pdf p. 39), immediately before the quoted sec. 3.2, describes closed word-final syllables in -k/-ng as 'receiving stress' and marks the final vowel with an acute in gemóeq, pucóeq, ussúeq, doyééng, while rule 3 on p.…

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim in the Verheijen 1986 PDF we hold at sec. 3.5, printed p. 9 = pdf p. 17, and the supporting loci (3.4.2.3, 3.3.1-2, 6.3.2.4) are also present and say what the record says (penult stress, schwa penult stressed, rightward shift under suffixation incl. pronominal suffixes, two lexical final-stress exceptions, Tanjoh caveat). (2) Deciding source: a 1986 Pacific Linguistics grammar sketch + dictionary by a seasoned field linguist; among Glottolog's 10 references for indo1317 it is the only English description with a stress section, and no phonology article, JIPA Illustration or instrumental study of Indonesian Bajau turned up in Glottolog, theses.fr, the Garuda journal portal, or the Badan Bahasa repository index. (3) downloaded now: Hapip, Darmansyah & Noor 1979 'Bahasa Bajau' (Kalimantan Bajau, 116 pp, via the Internet Archive) - sec. 3.2 says stress exists
